domain_label: Turlock Personal Care — Market, Demand, Saturation & Benchmark Economics
purpose: A method for sizing and reading the Turlock independent Personal Care market across its 25 cataloged businesses: quantifying the recurring-essential demand base (resident population, CSU Stanislaus youth, heritage event demand) that feeds the sector, explaining why each sub-category (barber, hair, nail, med spa, day spa, tattoo) saturates at the count it does, separating the low-capex distributor-fed group from the high-capex medical-procurement med-spa group, locating crowded sub-categories versus defensible white-space, accounting for the 2025 nail W-2 cost shock and for demand leakage to Modesto, and expressing every revenue, margin and market-size figure strictly as a labeled benchmark estimate (industry benchmark x observable size signal) rather than as a stated fact for any named business.
assumptions: no per-business revenue dataset is supplied; every dollar figure is a labeled benchmark estimate, never an actual reported figure for any named business such as Bliss Salon, Organic Nails, or Face&Beyond
the universe is the 25 verified Turlock independents in businesses.json (chains, mall/Walmart counters, and below-threshold solo/home/Instagram operators excluded), as of the 2026-06-30 snapshot

city/county/state figures (population ~72,500, median HH income ~$83,000, CSU enrollment, BarberCosmo and medical-director license requirements) are cited public facts or explicitly labeled derivations

sub-category revenue bands are published industry benchmarks (revenue per chair / per station / per provider / per artist) scaled by an observable Turlock size signal (chair count, station count, provider count, format), tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path
Modesto (~218,000, ~15 miles north) is the regional gravity center that caps Turlock's discretionary high-ticket ceiling (premium med spa, luxury spa, specialty tattoo)
coverage is reported as a FLOOR, not a ceiling: true on-the-ground density is higher than every per-10k figure shown because chains, counters, and gray-market solo operators are excluded
exclusions: per-sub-category supplier sourcing, inventory model, and equipment procurement detail — covered by the supply-chain KB
per-sub-category unit-economics, cost-structure line items, and go/no-go business-model detail — covered by the business-models KB
any claim of an actual, reported, or audited dollar revenue for a named business
chain and franchise personal-care (Great Clips / Sport Clips / Supercuts-type and mall/Walmart nail counters), which are outside the independents-only catalog
individual service pricing tactics, menu engineering, or marketing execution for a specific operator

competency_questions.question: What are the demand drivers that generate Turlock's recurring personal-care service demand, and how large is the resident base as a labeled estimate?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PC_DEMAND_BASE names the ~72,500 resident base at ~$83,000 median income, the ~8,455-UG CSU Stanislaus youth lift, and the recurring-essential cadence (barber every 2-4 weeks, nail fills every 2-3 weeks) that fixes the demand pool the 25 independents share, each tagged with source confidence

competency_questions.question: How does Turlock's heritage density (Assyrian, Portuguese/Azorean, Mexican, Punjabi/Sikh) raise the sector count above what population alone predicts?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HERITAGE_EVENT_DEMAND ties each community to wedding/quinceanera/festival event-beauty demand (updos, bridal, brow/lash, group bookings) and explains why a generic 72k town would carry fewer salon/nail/event chairs

competency_questions.question: How does the CSU Stanislaus student and young-male population shift demand toward particular sub-categories?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: STUDENT_YOUTH_DEMAND quantifies the ~8,455-UG term-time lift and shows which sub-categories (nails, brows/lashes, fades, first tattoos) it disproportionately supports plus the academic-calendar swing

competency_questions.question: Why does Turlock sustain roughly 25 independent personal-care businesses, and which forces set that equilibrium?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DEMAND_CEILING_CAP names the demand-governed cap (fixed recurring-cut/fill pool), the Modesto leakage trim, the online/at-home substitution trim, the med-spa licensing gate, and the heritage-event lift, tying the ~25 count to a demand-governed equilibrium

competency_questions.question: How is a per-sub-category benchmark revenue band built so it is an honest estimate and never a stated fact for a named business?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BENCHMARK_REVENUE_BANDS states the benchmark x size-signal method, gives the per-sub-category bands (barber, hair, nail, med spa, day spa, tattoo), and tags every band estimate-not-actual with confidence and a confirmation path

competency_questions.question: What does the businesses-per-10k saturation read show, and why is it a floor rather than a ceiling?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SATURATION_PER_10K gives the per-10k figures against national benchmarks (nail 0.97 vs ~3.4, tattoo 0.69 vs ~0.35) and states the floor caveat that excluded chains/counters/gray-market make true density higher

competency_questions.question: Which sub-categories are at or above local saturation and which retain headroom?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUBCATEGORY_SATURATION gives a per-sub-category catalog count vs realistic ceiling and a crowded / balanced / white-space read for each (nail and tattoo crowded, med spa and premium spa under-built)

competency_questions.question: How does Modesto's proximity cap Turlock's discretionary high-ticket ceiling?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MODESTO_LEAKAGE explains that premium med spa, luxury spa, and specialty tattoo leak ~15 miles north to a 3x-larger anchor, that Turlock keeps recurring-essential spend, and that the magnitude is the single largest unmeasured variable

competency_questions.question: How does the labor model (booth/chair rental vs W-2) shape sector economics, and what is the 2025 nail W-2 shock?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LABOR_MODEL_VARIABLE explains the booth/chair-rental dominance in barber/hair and NAIL_W2_SQUEEZE explains the AB5 manicurist carve-out expiry (1/1/2025) stacking a ~10-15% labor-cost step-up on already-weak nail pricing power

competency_questions.question: How does the capex spectrum and licensing structure split the sector and gate med-spa entry?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CAPEX_SPECTRUM contrasts low-capex barber/nail/tattoo/spa (~$1.5k-$6k/station) with med spa 10-50x higher ($50k-$150k devices), and LICENSING_BARRIER explains the physician medical-director wall that suppresses med-spa count to ~3

competency_questions.question: Where is the defensible white-space and how is it ranked once both demand and the entry wall are considered?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CROWDED_VS_WHITESPACE lists crowded sub-categories (do not add an 8th nail, 6th barber, 6th tattoo) and ranks white-space (med spa, premium destination spa, event/cultural beauty) each marked viable only after clearing the capital-and-licensure gate

competency_questions.question: How is a go/no-go market verdict reached for adding a sub-category, and how are the market reads refreshed when the underlying figures change?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ENTRY_GO_NOGO produces a verdict combining the saturation read, white-space rank, and capital/licensure gate (refusing demand-true but cost-gated additions), and MARKET_REVIEW_LOOP defines the refresh cadence and material-change triggers (new census/enrollment, a med spa or nail salon opens/closes, the W-2 cost step settles) that re-run the demand and saturation reads

glossary.definition: The habit-driven, recession-resilient rhythm anchoring the demand pool: barber every 2-4 weeks, nail fills every 2-3 weeks, basic women's cut/color every 6-10 weeks; small-ticket and sticky, distinct from the discretionary med-spa/spa/tattoo cadence. A pattern observation; ticket figures are labeled estimates.

A per-capita density read: cataloged independent count divided by (population/10,000), here divisor 7.25 for ~72,500 residents; reported as a FLOOR because chains, mall/Walmart counters, and below-threshold solo/home operators are excluded, so true density is higher than every figure shown.

The honest revenue-estimation method used throughout: take a published per-chair / per-station / per-provider / per-artist industry benchmark and scale it by an observable Turlock size signal (chair count, station count, provider count, format), yielding a band tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path.

The fixed local pool of recurring cut/fill demand that a ~72,500-resident, ~$83,000-median-income town supports; the primary cap on the sector count, such that adding an 8th nail salon mostly reshuffles share rather than growing the pie.

The siphoning of discretionary high-ticket demand (premium med spa, luxury spa days, specialty tattoo) ~15 miles north to Modesto (~218,000, 3x Turlock); Turlock retains recurring-essential convenience spend. Directionally certain but unmeasured — the single largest unknown in the analysis.

The compounded 2025 margin compression on the seven nail salons: California's AB5 booth-rental carve-out for manicurists expired 1/1/2025 forcing W-2 employment (a ~10-15%+ effective labor-cost step-up) on top of already weak, price-posted, walk-in-substitutable pricing power.

The entry-cost split: barber, nail, tattoo, and spa are low-capex (~$1,500-$6,000 per station/chair) while med spa is 10-50x higher ($50,000-$150,000 in devices), which governs the sector's competitive structure — low capex enables tattoo oversupply, high capex suppresses med-spa entry.

The binding med-spa entry wall: a physician (MD/DO) medical-director oversight structure plus six-figure device capex, why only ~3 med spas exist; white-space here must be read as high-barrier-under-built, not easy-to-enter.

Wedding / quinceanera / festival / formal-event beauty demand generated by Turlock's deep Assyrian, Portuguese/Azorean, Mexican, and Punjabi/Sikh communities (updos, bridal, brow/lash, group bookings) — the lone structural lift letting a 72k town carry more salon/nail/event capacity than population alone predicts.

The principle that the 25-business catalog is a floor not a ceiling: it deliberately excludes chains, mall/Walmart counters, and below-threshold solo/home/Instagram operators, so where a per-10k ratio reads thin (nail 0.97 vs ~3.4) that is a counting-method artifact, not demand headroom.

source_registry.description: labeled benchmark estimates and cited public facts for the Turlock independent Personal Care market, grounded in the personal_care deep-dive (DEEPDIVE.md), its upstream supply_ops / market_saturation / reconciled memos, and the 25-business source dataset (businesses.json); demand sizing uses census population and CSU Stanislaus enrollment, sub-category revenue bands use published barber/hair/nail/med-spa/tattoo per-unit benchmarks, and saturation/leakage reads use businesses-per-10k against national personal-care density figures
source_registry.citation_or_locator: California-Demographics / Census QuickFacts (Turlock ~72,500 pop, ~$83,000 median HH income, median age 34.9, 46% Hispanic, ~one-quarter Assyrian ancestry, ~7% Portuguese); CSU Stanislaus IEA (~8,455 UG, ~9,300 total, Fall 2024); Poidata/IBISWorld (US nail-salon count ~113k-118k -> ~3.4/10k); ResearchAndMarkets 2024 (US tattoo studios ~11,600 -> ~0.35/10k); joinblvd/Booksy/Vagaro/Trafft/Kentley/Statista (barber, hair, nail per-unit revenue benchmarks); AmSpa 2024 Medical Spa State of the Industry (~$1.4M avg single-location, national estimate); CA BarberCosmo establishment/licensure FAQs; PBFC/NAILS/CalMatters (AB5 manicurist W-2 transition effective 1/1/2025); personal_care DEEPDIVE.md, businesses.json

nodes.definition: Catalog the structural demand engines that feed Turlock's recurring personal-care spend: a ~72,500 resident base at ~$83,000 median household income and median age 34.9, plus the ~8,455-undergraduate (term-time ~9,300 total) CSU Stanislaus population that disproportionately consumes nails, brows/lashes, fades and first tattoos. Income sits above the Stanislaus County average but well below coastal-CA metros, so the town supports volume formats (value nail/barber) more readily than premium-only formats — exactly the observed mix across the 25 independents. These overlapping populations, not the resident count alone, set the demand the sector shares.

excluded: splitting demand into recurring vs discretionary cadence (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a population, enrollment, or median-income figure is refreshed

pros.claim: Naming the resident base plus the CSU youth lift explains a service-demand mix a population count alone cannot
pros.example: the young-male CSU base supports five barber shops a generic 72k town would not

cons.claim: Overlapping resident and student populations risk double-counting demand if treated as independent pools
cons.example: a CSU student who also lives in Turlock counted twice inflates the apparent base

failure_modes: treating CSU enrollment as net-new demand rather than partly overlapping residents
reading above-county income as premium-capable when it is below coastal metros and favors volume formats
acceptance_tests: the resident base (~72,500), median income (~$83,000) and CSU UG figure (~8,455) are each stated with their source and confidence, and the volume-over-premium format implication is drawn explicitly
revisit_triggers: a census or ACS demographic refresh
a CSU Stanislaus enrollment release
a median-income update that shifts the volume-vs-premium read

nodes.definition: Explain Turlock's lone count-expanding demand feature: unusually deep heritage communities each generate wedding / quinceanera / festival / formal-event beauty demand a generic 72k town would not carry. Turlock holds an Assyrian community of roughly one-quarter of the city (4th-highest Assyrian-ancestry share in the U.S.), a ~7% Portuguese/Azorean base, a near-majority Mexican base, and a Punjabi/Sikh community — each anchoring formal updos, bridal, brow/lash, henna-adjacent services and group bookings. This event demand sustains more salon/nail/event capacity than population alone predicts and is a defensible, under-formalized niche national chains structurally cannot serve.

included: Assyrian, Portuguese, Mexican, Punjabi/Sikh community shares
excluded: the dollar size of each community's spend

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a heritage-community share or event-demand pattern changes

pros.claim: Mapping community to event-beauty demand explains a salon/nail count national density models under-predict
pros.example: Assyrian and Mexican wedding/quinceanera bookings sustain bridal and updo capacity a 72k town would not

cons.claim: Ancestry share is a crude proxy for event spend, since communities differ in frequency and ticket
cons.example: a large but value-oriented Mexican base lifts volume formats but caps event-beauty revenue

failure_modes: assuming ancestry share converts linearly to event-beauty revenue
treating event demand as year-round rather than season/calendar-concentrated
acceptance_tests: each of the four heritage communities is tied to at least one event-beauty service with its cited population share, and the count-lift-above-population claim is stated explicitly
revisit_triggers: an ancestry/demographic data refresh
a heritage community grows or contracts via migration
an event-beauty-anchored salon or nail business opens or closes

nodes.definition: Isolate how the CSU Stanislaus student body (~8,455 undergraduates Fall 2024, rebounding but not booming) and the young-resident base reshape demand by sub-category. Term-time students and young residents disproportionately lift nails, brows/lashes, fades and first tattoos, while creating an academic-calendar swing — demand softens in summer and over breaks. This segment is a primary reason barber and tattoo run at-or-above local saturation for a 72k town: the CSU plus heavy Hispanic young-male base supports five barber shops and a tattoo density running ~2x the national per-capita benchmark.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a CSU enrollment or youth-demand pattern figure changes

pros.claim: Isolating youth demand explains barber and tattoo density a resident-only read would call oversupply without cause
pros.example: first-tattoo and fade demand from the CSU and young-male base supports counts national density flags as high

cons.claim: Youth demand is calendar-fragile, so sub-categories over-built on it face summer/break troughs
cons.example: a campus-adjacent nail or brow studio that empties between spring and fall terms

failure_modes: treating peak-term youth traffic as year-round baseline
ignoring that enrollment is rebounding, not booming, so the lift is bounded
acceptance_tests: the youth lift is tied to specific sub-categories (nails, brows/lashes, fades, first tattoos) with the ~8,455-UG figure, and the academic-calendar swing is named
revisit_triggers: a CSU Stanislaus enrollment release moves the figure materially
a campus-housing or commuter-pattern change shifts youth demand

nodes.definition: Establish the demand split that anchors the whole analysis: Personal Care is two demand rhythms sharing a storefront aesthetic. Recurring-essential — barber (every 2-4 weeks), nail fills (every 2-3 weeks), basic women's cut/color (every 6-10 weeks) — is sticky, habit-driven, recession-resilient, small-ticket ($25-$40 men's cut, $35-$60 mani-pedi, labeled estimates). Discretionary/aspirational — med-spa injectables (every 3-4 months), day-spa massage/facials, lash extensions, tattoos — is higher-ticket ($150-$700+), income-elastic, first cut when budgets tighten. The count is anchored by the recurring floor; the discretionary tier is what leaks to Modesto and is gated by capital and licensure.

included: the recurring-essential vs discretionary cadence and ticket split
excluded: the dollar pool sizing (its own node)
the Modesto leakage mechanism detail (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a cadence, ticket benchmark, or elasticity assumption changes

pros.claim: Splitting demand into two rhythms explains why the count is anchored by recurring cadence and the margin/leakage story sits in the discretionary tier
pros.example: a $35 mani-pedi habit fills chairs reliably while a $400 injectable visit is income-elastic and leakage-prone

cons.claim: Some businesses straddle both rhythms, so a clean two-tier split can mislabel a hybrid
cons.example: Bliss and Organic Nails carry both recurring nail/hair and discretionary spa services

failure_modes: treating discretionary med-spa cadence as recurring and over-counting its demand floor
ignoring that recession resilience differs sharply between the two tiers
acceptance_tests: both tiers are named with their cadence and ticket range (labeled estimate), the recession-resilience contrast is stated, and the leak/gate consequence is assigned to the discretionary tier
revisit_triggers: a macro shift changes discretionary elasticity
a ticket-price benchmark is refreshed
a hybrid business reclassifies its primary cadence

nodes.definition: Size the recurring service-demand pool the 25 independents share as a labeled estimate, not a measured figure. The pool is the product of the ~72,500-resident base (plus the partly-overlapping CSU youth segment) times recurring per-capita visit frequency at the labeled per-visit tickets from the demand split (men's cut $25-$40, mani-pedi $35-$60). The defensible output is a demand-volume read (how many recurring cut/fill chairs the town sustains), not a precise dollar market size, because per-business revenue is not public. Student and heritage-event spend partly overlaps and partly adds to the resident pool rather than stacking cleanly on top of it; the confirmation path is local sales-tax / licensing-density data.

included: resident-base x recurring-frequency x labeled-ticket pool math
excluded: the per-chair average trap (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a population, frequency, ticket, or sales-tax figure is refreshed

pros.claim: A transparent population-x-frequency-x-ticket method gives a defensible demand pool without quoting any business
pros.example: expressing the pool as recurring chairs the town sustains lets a reader audit the estimate end to end

cons.claim: Per-capita frequency and ticket are themselves estimates, so the pool is a range not a point
cons.example: nail-fill frequency varies widely by segment, widening the pool band

failure_modes: presenting the pool as a measured dollar market size rather than a demand-volume estimate
stacking student and heritage-event spend fully on top of the resident pool and double-counting
acceptance_tests: the pool is stated as a labeled estimate with its population x frequency x ticket derivation, framed as demand-volume (chairs) with a confidence level and a confirmation path, tagged estimate-not-actual
revisit_triggers: a population or enrollment refresh
a recurring-frequency or ticket benchmark update
local sales-tax or licensing-density data becomes available

nodes.definition: Build the per-sub-category revenue bands that are the primary, most defensible revenue view, every one a labeled estimate (published benchmark x observable Turlock size signal), never an actual figure for a named business. Representative bands (annual, estimate-not-actual): barber $90k-$280k (per chair x 3-6 chairs); men's grooming $130k-$300k (chairs + product attach); hair salon house $150k-$500k with booth renters individually ~$40k-$90k take; nail $150k-$420k (per station x 6-12); med spa $350k-$1.2M (per injector-provider, injectable-led, against the ~$1.4M AmSpa national single-location estimate); day spa $120k-$350k (per treatment room); tattoo $60k-$300k (per artist x 1-5). Each pairs revenue with its cost/margin reality (thin nail net, capital-gated med-spa net) so high gross is never read as high profit.

excluded: the per-chair average critique (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a benchmark source or measured size signal changes

pros.claim: Per-sub-category bands anchored to published benchmarks give a planning estimate without quoting any operator
pros.example: a barber band of $90k-$280k from per-chair revenue x chair count is auditable and business-agnostic

cons.claim: Bands rest on national benchmarks and unobserved size signals, so any single business can sit far outside its band
cons.example: a high-volume strip-center nail salon could exceed the $420k top while a small one falls below the floor

failure_modes: attaching a band to a named business (e.g., Bliss or Face&Beyond) as if it were that business's revenue
dropping the cost/margin pairing so a high-gross med-spa band reads as high-profit
acceptance_tests: each major sub-category has a low/high band derived as benchmark x a stated size signal, tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence and confirmation path, and paired with its cost/margin caveat
revisit_triggers: a published benchmark source updates
an observable size signal (chairs, stations, providers, artists) is measured for a sub-category
local distribution data lands

nodes.definition: Correct a common misread: dividing a sub-category benchmark total by the catalog count produces a per-business arithmetic mean that is not a typical business. The mean is pulled up by a right tail — full-service hair houses, multi-injector med spas, and high-volume nail strip-centers — and is inflated further if a high-gross band is read without its thin-net caveat. The typical Turlock independent sits in the lower-to-middle of its sub-category band (e.g., a 1-3 artist tattoo studio in the $60k-$150k portion, a small 2-chair barber below the $90k floor). The per-business average should be read as a low-confidence ceiling-of-plausibility, with the per-sub-category bands the primary view; local outlet-level data would resolve it.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: outlet-level revenue distribution data appears

pros.claim: Naming the per-business-average trap stops a reader concluding the typical Turlock shop grosses the band midpoint or above
pros.example: showing the mean sits above most 1-3 artist tattoo studios exposes it as tail-driven

cons.claim: Emphasizing the correction can make the directional pool sanity-check seem worthless when it still has value
cons.example: discarding the average entirely loses a useful count-vs-demand consistency check

failure_modes: quoting a band midpoint as the typical business
presenting a single point estimate instead of the typical-business range within the band
acceptance_tests: the per-business average is labeled a low-confidence mean, its right-tail cause is stated, and the typical-business placement within each sub-category band is given as the primary read
revisit_triggers: outlet-level revenue distribution data becomes available
a per-sub-category band is revised

nodes.definition: Establish the labor model as the sector's defining economic variable. Booth/chair-rental dominates barber and hair: owners rent stations to independently-licensed pros who keep service revenue, issue a 1099 for rent, carry their own insurance, and book their own clients — Salon Two Zero Nine explicitly advertises independent stylists and private suites. This converts the owner's revenue to predictable rent (commonly ~$150-$350/week per chair, low-confidence estimate) rather than service margin and shifts COGS, scheduling and client risk onto the renter, so owner-level and operator-level economics diverge and must not be summed. Owner-operator / small W-2 crews dominate single-chair shops and walk-in tattoo studios; med spa runs physician-supervised RN/NP/PA injectors.

excluded: the 2025 nail W-2 shock specifically (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a worker-classification rule or chair-rent benchmark changes

pros.claim: Foregrounding the labor model explains why a hair house's revenue is rent collected, not service margin
pros.example: Salon Two Zero Nine's suite/booth-rent model converts owner economics to rent and offloads COGS to renters

cons.claim: Local rent figures are unpublished, so the per-chair rent benchmark is low confidence
cons.example: the ~$150-$350/week chair rent is a regional pro-forum figure, not a verified Turlock rate

failure_modes: summing the hair house band and the per-renter take band as if they were additive revenue
treating booth-rent owner economics as service-margin economics
acceptance_tests: the booth/chair-rental model is described for barber and hair with the rent-vs-service-margin inversion and the explicit do-not-sum caveat on house vs per-renter revenue
revisit_triggers: a worker-classification rule changes
a local chair-rent benchmark becomes available
a named salon shifts between rental and W-2 models

nodes.definition: Model the sector's most important current operating dynamic: a compounded margin squeeze on the seven nail salons that neither upstream memo states alone. Two forces stack. First, a structural cost increase — California's AB5 booth-rental carve-out for manicurists expired 1/1/2025, forcing nail techs to be W-2 employees (hair/skin/barber pros retain the Borello carve-out), adding ~10-15%+ to effective labor cost via payroll tax, workers' comp, admin and PAGA-misclassification exposure, and disproportionately affecting the Vietnamese-immigrant labor base. Second, weak pricing power — price-posted, walk-in-substitutable, low-differentiation competition with little ability to pass cost through. Combined, this is compounded compression in 2025; per-business magnitude is unknown.

excluded: the general booth-rental model (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a worker-classification rule or nail cost-absorption signal changes

pros.claim: Stacking the structural cost increase on weak pricing power gives the decision-grade nail read
pros.example: a forced W-2 step-up landing on price-posted walk-in nail competition compounds the margin hit

cons.claim: The ~10-15% step-up and per-business absorption are estimates, unobservable from public data
cons.example: how each of the seven nail salons absorbs the cost (price rise, hour cuts, owner absorption, informal non-compliance) is unknown

failure_modes: treating the W-2 step-up as a one-time event rather than a structural margin change
applying the manicurist W-2 rule to hair/skin/barber pros who retain the Borello carve-out
acceptance_tests: the 1/1/2025 manicurist W-2 transition, the ~10-15%+ labor-cost step-up, and the weak-pricing-power compounding are all stated, with the per-business magnitude flagged unknown
revisit_triggers: a further worker-classification or PAGA enforcement change
evidence on how local nail salons absorbed the cost
a nail-salon ticket-price benchmark update

nodes.definition: Give the businesses-per-10k saturation read using cataloged independent count divided by (population/10,000), divisor 7.25 for ~72,500 residents — explicitly a FLOOR because chains, mall/Walmart counters, and home/booth-rent solo operators below the catalog threshold are excluded. Per-10k against national benchmarks: nail 0.97 vs ~3.4 (Poidata/IBIS estimate) — below national on independents-only but locally crowded in lived terms; tattoo 0.69 vs ~0.35 (ResearchAndMarkets estimate) — ~2x national, a clear oversupply signal; barber 0.69-0.83, crowded for the town; med spa 0.41, under-built; sector total 3.45, moderate. cons.claim: Independents-only per-10k understates true density and can be misread as headroom

nodes.definition: Explain why Turlock sustains roughly 25 independents as a demand-governed, not supply-governed, equilibrium. A fixed local demand pool supports a finite number of recurring-essential chairs, and that demand ceiling — not supply-chain friction — is the primary cap; supply chain and capex explain the mix and margins of who exists, not the count. Forces stack: the demand ceiling caps the count (nail and barber at/near local saturation, so an 8th nail salon reshuffles share); Modesto leakage and online/at-home substitution trim it; licensing gates only the high-capex med-spa tier; and heritage-event demand is the lone offsetting lift. ~25 is where the recurring floor is filled, nail/barber/tattoo run at-or-above saturation, and med spa / premium spa stay under-built behind a capital-and-licensure wall.

included: the stacked forces (ceiling, leakage, substitution, licensing, heritage lift)
excluded: the per-sub-category saturation reads (its own node)
the Modesto mechanism detail (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: one of the stacked equilibrium forces shifts

pros.claim: Framing 25 as a demand-governed equilibrium resists both over-building and under-building conclusions
pros.example: it explains why supply-chain ease does not raise the count when the demand pool is full

cons.claim: An equilibrium framing can imply false stability when trends (enrollment, the W-2 shock, med-spa growth) are moving
cons.example: treating 25 as fixed when a med-spa entrant could clear the wall and lift the sustainable count

failure_modes: attributing the count to supply-chain friction when demand is the binding cap
ignoring that the equilibrium drifts as the stacked forces change
acceptance_tests: the demand-governed thesis is stated, all stacked forces (ceiling, Modesto leakage, online/at-home substitution, med-spa licensing, heritage-event lift) are named, and each is tied to the ~25-count outcome
revisit_triggers: the demand pool, Modesto draw, substitution, licensing barrier, or heritage demand shifts materially
the independent count moves away from ~25

nodes.definition: Give the per-sub-category saturation read by setting the catalog count against a realistic ceiling for a ~72,500 town: nail 7 (per-10k 0.97) — locally crowded, low-differentiation, walk-in-substitutable, an 8th adds a chair to a saturated room; barber 5 (+1 grooming hybrid) — saturated for the size, differentiated on brand/vibe and the CSU fade niche; tattoo 5 (~2x national density) — clear oversupply, low per-station capex enables it, top-end work leaks to Modesto/Bay Area; hair 3 full-service — undercounted, booth-rent stylists inside Bliss/Salon 209/suites are not separate rows so real density is higher; med spa 3 — white-space-ish/under-built behind the entry wall; day spa 1 standalone — thin, mostly bundled into salons. Crowded: nail, barber, tattoo. Under-built: med spa, premium spa.

excluded: the white-space ranking and entry wall (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a sub-category count or anchoring demand changes

pros.claim: A count-vs-ceiling read makes each sub-category's saturation or headroom legible at a glance
pros.example: nail 7 and tattoo 5 read as crowded while med spa 3 reads as under-built

cons.claim: Sub-category ceilings are themselves estimates, so a crowded/room read can flip if the ceiling is mis-set
cons.example: the hair count understates true density because booth-rent stylists are not separate rows

failure_modes: reading a primary-category count as the full picture when booth-rent stylists or spa secondaries shift it
treating an estimated ceiling as a hard cap
acceptance_tests: each major sub-category has a catalog count, a realistic ceiling, and a crowded/balanced/white-space read, with the hair-undercount and tattoo-oversupply calls stated
revisit_triggers: a business opens or closes in the catalog
a demographic shift changes a sub-category's anchoring demand
Modesto leakage for a sub-category is measured

nodes.definition: Model the Modesto ceiling on the discretionary tier. Modesto (~218,000, three times Turlock's population, ~15 miles north) is the regional retail/medical gravity center, and higher-ticket specialty demand — premium med spa, plastics-adjacent aesthetics, luxury spa days, specialty tattoo artists — leaks north. Turlock keeps the recurring-essential, convenience-driven spend and loses the make-a-day-of-it discretionary spend. This is inferred from Modesto's size and retail role; no published Turlock-specific leakage study was found, so the magnitude is the single largest unmeasured variable in the analysis — directionally certain but quantitatively unknown. The fine-detail consequence is that Turlock's med-spa and premium-spa ceilings are lower than local demand math alone would suggest.

included: the Modesto anchor effect on discretionary spend
excluded: the online/at-home substitution channel (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: Modesto cross-shop behavior or its discretionary scene changes

pros.claim: Naming Modesto leakage explains the discretionary ceiling demand math alone cannot
pros.example: premium injectable and luxury-spa demand splits north to Modesto's larger scene, capping Turlock's med-spa/premium-spa ceiling

cons.claim: Leakage is inferred from proximity and scale, not measured, so its magnitude is uncertain
cons.example: without a cross-shop study the exact share of Turlock discretionary spend going to Modesto is unknown

failure_modes: treating the leakage estimate as a measured figure
applying the discretionary-leakage logic to recurring-essential formats Modesto does not actually draw
acceptance_tests: the Modesto anchor is quantified by population ratio (~3x) and distance (~15 miles), tied to discretionary high-ticket leakage, and flagged as the single largest unmeasured variable with its confirmation path
revisit_triggers: a Turlock-vs-Modesto cross-shop leakage study is done
Modesto's med-spa/spa/tattoo scene expands or contracts
a new premium discretionary entrant opens in Turlock

nodes.definition: Account for the online/DTC and at-home substitution that caps per-visit spend and the number of chairs a fixed population supports. Grooming products, at-home gel/dip kits, clipper/DIY culture, and at-home skincare cannibalize the product-attach and low-end-service margin — exactly the higher-margin retail attach that men's grooming (Noblemens' pomade/beard oil) and day spas (retail beauty product) rely on. The substitution effect is directional and qualitative; its magnitude is unknown. It is one of the trims (alongside Modesto leakage) that pulls the equilibrium count below what the raw recurring-demand pool would otherwise support.

included: the product-attach and low-end-service margin cannibalization
excluded: the Modesto regional leakage channel (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a DTC/at-home substitution or retail-attach signal changes

pros.claim: Naming at-home substitution explains a per-visit and attach-margin cap a pure-demand read would miss
pros.example: at-home gel/dip kits and clipper culture trim low-end nail and barber margin

cons.claim: The substitution magnitude is unmeasured, so it stays directional not sized
cons.example: knowing at-home kits cannibalize attach margin does not say by how much without sales data

failure_modes: treating at-home substitution as negligible because it is hard to size
double-counting it with Modesto leakage as if they were the same channel
acceptance_tests: the at-home/DTC substitution channels are named, tied to the product-attach and low-end-service margin, and flagged as a directional, unsized trim on the equilibrium count
revisit_triggers: a DTC/at-home category shift changes substitution
a retail-attach benchmark becomes available
a named business reports an attach-revenue change

nodes.definition: Define the capex spectrum that governs the sector's competitive structure in one line: barber, nail, tattoo and spa are low-capex (~$1,500-$6,000 per station/chair) while med spa is 10-50x higher ($50,000-$150,000 in devices), which is why leasing-not-buying is the common cash-flow workaround there. This single fact explains the structure: low capex enables the tattoo oversupply the market observes (5 studios, ~2x national density), while high capex plus licensure suppresses med-spa entry into otherwise-attractive white-space. All capex figures are labeled estimates (vendor/industry pricing, low-to-moderate confidence), not actuals for any named business.

excluded: the medical-director licensure detail (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a capex or leasing-market benchmark changes

pros.claim: The capex spectrum explains both tattoo oversupply and med-spa scarcity in one structural fact
pros.example: ~$2k-$6k/station tattoo entry enables the ~2x-density oversupply while $50k-$150k med-spa devices suppress entry

cons.claim: Capex figures are vendor/industry estimates with wide ranges, not verified local costs
cons.example: med-spa device cost swings widely by modality and buy-vs-lease choice

failure_modes: treating low capex as the only driver of tattoo oversupply without the demand and reputation context
reading med-spa high capex as the sole barrier when licensure also gates it
acceptance_tests: the low-capex band (~$1.5k-$6k/station) and the med-spa band ($50k-$150k devices) are both stated as labeled estimates and tied to the tattoo-oversupply / med-spa-suppression structure
revisit_triggers: a device or station-equipment pricing benchmark updates
a leasing-market change alters the med-spa workaround
a low-capex entrant opens in a crowded sub-category

nodes.definition: Distinguish the routine licensing gate from the binding one. CA BarberCosmo (BarberCosmo) licensure gates barbers, cosmetologists, estheticians and manicurists plus an establishment license with sanitation/plumbing minimums — a real but routine gate that does not by itself cap the count. The binding barrier is med spa: a physician medical-director oversight structure (corporate-practice-of-medicine compliance, injectables as FDA-regulated prescription products via authorized medical distributors, medical malpractice) plus six-figure device capex is the single biggest entry barrier, explaining why only ~3 med spas exist despite attractive category economics. Tattoo is regulatorily constrained too (Safe Body Art Act, county Body Art Facility permit), but its low capex still permits oversupply. Med-spa white-space is therefore high-barrier-under-built, not easy-to-enter.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a medical-director, corporate-practice, or BarberCosmo rule changes

pros.claim: Separating routine from binding licensure pinpoints why med spa is suppressed while barber/nail are not
pros.example: the physician medical-director wall, not BarberCosmo, is why only ~3 med spas exist

cons.claim: Licensure detail can imply the med-spa barrier is purely regulatory when capital is co-binding
cons.example: the medical-director wall and six-figure device capex jointly suppress entry, not licensure alone

failure_modes: reading med-spa white-space as easy-to-enter because demand looks unmet
treating the routine BarberCosmo gate as a count-capping barrier
acceptance_tests: the routine BarberCosmo gate and the binding med-spa medical-director gate are both stated, the ~3 med-spa count is tied to the binding gate, and the high-barrier-under-built framing is made explicit
revisit_triggers: a CA medical-director or corporate-practice rule changes
a BarberCosmo establishment requirement changes
a med-spa entrant clears the wall

nodes.definition: Locate and rank the competitive structure with the entry wall applied. Crowded (share-shuffle, not pie-growth): do not add an 8th nail salon (saturated, margin-compressed by the W-2 squeeze), a 6th barber (saturated, chain-pressured at the value end), or a 6th tattoo studio (~2x national density, reputation-gated, top-end leaking north). Defensible white-space, ranked: (1) med spa — favorable national economics and clear premium-aesthetics leakage to Modesto, viable only for a well-capitalized operator who clears the physician-oversight + six-figure-capex wall and out-competes Modesto on convenience/trust; (2) premium destination spa — recapture the day-spa spend leaking north; (3) event/cultural beauty — Assyrian/Portuguese/Hispanic/Punjabi wedding-and-formal demand no chain can serve. Each white-space is demand-true but capital-and-licensure-gated.

included: the capital-and-licensure gate qualifier on each
excluded: the per-decision go/no-go verdict (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a white-space opening is entered or its demand/entry-wall changes

pros.claim: Ranking white-space with the entry wall applied prevents recommending a demand-true but un-enterable opening
pros.example: med spa ranks first on demand yet is viable only after clearing the medical-director and six-figure-capex wall

cons.claim: A ranked list can read as a recommendation when each opening still needs an operator's own feasibility check
cons.example: event/cultural beauty ranks high but needs a specific operator's capacity to deliver group bookings

failure_modes: listing med-spa white-space on demand alone without the medical-director and capital gate
recommending an addition in a crowded sub-category because its heritage anchor looks durable
acceptance_tests: the do-not-add list (8th nail, 6th barber, 6th tattoo) and at least three ranked white-space openings (med spa, premium spa, event/cultural beauty) are given, each white-space marked viable only after the capital-and-licensure gate clears
revisit_triggers: a white-space opening is entered locally
a demographic or leakage shift changes an opening's demand
the capital or licensure gate changes

nodes.definition: Size (as a flagged unknown) the gray-market / below-catalog operator class that the 25-business catalog deliberately excludes: solo/home/Instagram-booked stylists and nail/lash techs, plus mall/Walmart counters and value chains. This class draws on the same CosmoProf/SalonCentric/DTK distributor channels and fragments share as a real competitor, but neither upstream memo counts it or models its draw, making it the most material missing supply input. Its existence is the reason the per-10k figures are a floor: where a ratio reads thin (nail 0.97 vs ~3.4), restoring this excluded class lifts true density toward or past national benchmarks. Its count and distributor draw are unknown.

excluded: the cataloged per-10k figures themselves (its own node)
the coverage-honesty discipline statement (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a gray-market sizing or platform-prevalence signal changes

pros.claim: Flagging the gray-market class explains why the per-10k figures are a floor and where true density hides
pros.example: home/Instagram nail and lash techs lift true nail density toward the ~3.4 national benchmark

cons.claim: The class is unsized, so its competitive draw stays qualitative
cons.example: neither memo counts home/booth operators, so the share they fragment is unknown

failure_modes: ignoring the gray-market class and treating the catalog as the full competitive field
double-counting it against the cataloged independents
acceptance_tests: the below-catalog operator class is named, tied to the same distributor channels, flagged unsized, and connected to the per-10k floor caveat
revisit_triggers: a gray-market sizing study or licensing-roster cross-check becomes available
a platform shift changes home/Instagram operator prevalence

nodes.definition: Enforce the binding honesty discipline across every dollar figure: per-business revenue is not public, so no dollar figure is ever stated as an actual reported figure for a named business such as Bliss, Organic Nails, Aesthetic Lab or Face&Beyond. Every sub-category dollar band is a labeled benchmark estimate (published benchmark x observable size signal) tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path; every high-gross band is paired with its thin-net / capital-gated caveat; city/county/state figures (population, income, license requirements) are cited public facts or labeled derivations; supplier-to-named-business links are representative inference unless self-disclosed (Organic Nails' SNS dipping, Face&Beyond's multi-brand injectables). Two national-benchmark-as-fact drifts must stay tagged: the med-spa ~$1.4M AmSpa average and the nail ~$34 revenue/capita Statista figure are national estimates, not Turlock facts.

excluded: the specific band values (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new dollar figure is introduced or an actual datum becomes available

pros.claim: A single explicit guardrail keeps every downstream number honest and auditable
pros.example: tagging the med-spa ~$1.4M average a national estimate prevents it reading as a Turlock fact

cons.claim: Heavy labeling can make the analysis read as hedged and lower its perceived usefulness
cons.example: a reader wanting a single revenue number for a named salon is frustrated by a band tagged low-confidence

failure_modes: letting a sub-category band attach to a named business as that business's revenue
stating the med-spa ~$1.4M or nail ~$34/capita national benchmark as a bare Turlock fact
acceptance_tests: every dollar figure in any node is a labeled estimate or a cited public fact, no named-business actual revenue appears, each high-gross band carries its thin-net caveat, and the med-spa ~$1.4M and nail ~$34/capita figures are explicitly tagged national estimates
revisit_triggers: a new node introduces a dollar figure
a public-fact source is added or updated
an actual revenue datum becomes available to replace an estimate

nodes.definition: Enforce the coverage-honesty discipline: the 25-business catalog is a FLOOR, not a ceiling, because it deliberately excludes chains, mall/Walmart counters, and below-threshold solo/home/Instagram operators, so true on-the-ground density is higher than every per-10k figure shown. Where a ratio reads thin — most importantly nail 0.97 vs ~3.4 — that is a counting-method artifact, not demand headroom, and must never be cited as evidence to add capacity. Source confidence also varies by business (several rows rest on Yelp/Instagram/Facebook listings at medium confidence: Jack's, The Fade Room, Moezart, Rebelucio, Third Eye, Advance Med Spa, Jennifer Nail), so the size signals feeding the revenue bands are themselves estimates. This is a static 2026-06-30 snapshot.

included: the per-business confidence variance and snapshot caveat
excluded: the dollar-figure honesty discipline (its own node)
the cataloged per-10k figures (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a coverage source is added or a business row is verified

pros.claim: A coverage-floor rule prevents a thin per-10k ratio being misread as room to grow
pros.example: the nail 0.97-vs-3.4 gap is flagged a counting artifact, not headroom, blocking a false add signal

cons.claim: Constant floor-caveating can make every density read feel non-committal
cons.example: a reader wanting a clean saturation verdict is slowed by the repeated floor qualifier

failure_modes: citing a thin per-10k ratio as headroom despite the floor caveat
treating medium-confidence aggregator-sourced rows as fully verified size signals
acceptance_tests: the floor-not-ceiling rule is stated, the nail-gap-is-an-artifact correction is made, and the per-business source-confidence variance plus the static-snapshot date are both flagged
revisit_triggers: a chain/counter/gray-market source is added that changes true density
a medium-confidence business row is independently verified
the snapshot is refreshed past 2026-06-30

nodes.definition: Produce the market go/no-go verdict for adding a given sub-category, composing the saturation read, the white-space rank, the demand-ceiling logic, and the capital-and-licensure gate into one decision. The merged rule: do not add an 8th nail salon, a 6th barber, or a 6th tattoo studio (all at or above local saturation; an entrant reshuffles share into a margin-compressed nail field or a reputation-gated tattoo field); the defensible headroom is med spa (only after clearing the physician-oversight + six-figure-capex wall and out-competing Modesto), premium destination spa (recapture the day-spa spend leaking north), and event/cultural beauty (a format no chain can serve). A demand-true opening that fails the capital-and-licensure gate is a no-go until the gate clears; every revenue rationale must travel as a labeled estimate under the honesty guardrail.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a saturation, cost-step, or entry-gate input to the verdict changes

pros.claim: Composing all reads into one verdict gives an actionable add/avoid call instead of scattered signals
pros.example: the verdict says no to an 8th nail salon but yes to a med spa once the medical-director and capital wall are cleared

cons.claim: A single verdict can over-simplify a sub-category whose demand and entry gate point opposite ways
cons.example: premium spa has demand headroom yet still needs a destination-concept feasibility pass before a clean yes

failure_modes: issuing a yes on demand headroom while ignoring an unmet capital-and-licensure gate
recommending an addition in a crowded sub-category because its heritage or youth anchor looks durable
acceptance_tests: the verdict for a proposed sub-category combines its saturation read, white-space rank, and capital-and-licensure gate status, refuses any demand-true but cost-gated addition, and names the do-not-add sub-categories
revisit_triggers: a saturation read, the W-2 cost step, or the entry gate feeding the verdict changes
a previously gated opening clears its capital-and-licensure gate

nodes.definition: Define the loop that keeps the market reads current. A fixed refresh cadence (re-run on each major data release) plus material-change triggers — a census/ACS demographic or CSU Stanislaus enrollment refresh, a med spa or nail/barber/tattoo business opening or closing, the 2025 nail W-2 cost step settling into observable absorption, a national personal-care density or revenue benchmark update, a CA medical-director or worker-classification rule change, or a Turlock-vs-Modesto leakage study — that send the analysis back through SERVICE_DEMAND_POOL and the saturation reads. Without this loop the 2026-06-30 snapshot silently goes stale as enrollment rebounds, the nail W-2 squeeze plays out, and med spa compounds nationally as a category.

included: re-entry into pool sizing and saturation

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a material-change trigger fires or the cadence is tuned

pros.claim: A trigger list keeps the lowest-confidence reads (Modesto leakage, nail cost absorption) on a path to resolution
pros.example: a leakage study or post-W-2 absorption evidence fires the loop and replaces estimates with observed reads

cons.claim: Too-frequent refresh churns the reads without new signal, since most inputs update only annually
cons.example: re-sizing the demand pool monthly when census and enrollment move only yearly wastes effort

failure_modes: no cadence set so the snapshot ages silently past its trend assumptions
ignoring a fired trigger (a med-spa entrant) and continuing on stale saturation reads
acceptance_tests: a refresh cadence and an explicit material-change trigger list exist, each routing back to SERVICE_DEMAND_POOL and the saturation reads, with the leakage study and post-W-2 absorption named as high-leverage triggers
revisit_triggers: a material-change trigger fires
the cadence proves too frequent or too sparse for how the inputs actually update

conflict_axes.name: demand_headroom_vs_entry_wall
conflict_axes.description: A sub-category can be demand-true white space yet be walled off by the physician medical-director structure and six-figure capex, so demand and feasibility point opposite ways.
poles: block on the unmet capital-and-licensure gate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat a demand-true opening as a no-go until its entry wall clears; demand never overrides the medical-director and capital gate

conflict_axes.name: per_business_average_vs_typical_business
conflict_axes.description: A per-business mean drawn from the bands and the typical-business read within a band cannot both describe a representative operator.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the per-sub-category band is the primary view; the per-business average is a low-confidence ceiling pulled up by a right tail

conflict_axes.name: independents_only_count_vs_true_density
conflict_axes.description: The independents-only per-10k count and true on-the-ground density diverge because chains, counters, and gray-market operators are excluded.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: report the per-10k as a floor; a thin ratio like nail 0.97-vs-3.4 is a counting artifact, not headroom, until the excluded class is restored

conflict_axes.name: heritage_lift_vs_modesto_ceiling
conflict_axes.description: Heritage event demand pushes the count above population prediction while Modesto's gravity pulls discretionary demand away and caps it.
poles: count rises on heritage event demand
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: heritage lifts the ceiling for salon/nail/event capacity; Modesto caps discretionary med-spa/premium-spa; apply each to the tier it governs

conflict_axes.name: recurring_resilience_vs_discretionary_elasticity
conflict_axes.description: The recurring-essential floor is recession-resilient while the discretionary tier is income-elastic and first-cut, so a single demand read mislabels one of them.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: anchor the count to the recurring floor and locate the leakage/margin risk in the discretionary tier

conflict_axes.name: low_capex_oversupply_vs_high_capex_scarcity
conflict_axes.description: Low per-station capex enables tattoo oversupply while six-figure med-spa capex plus licensure suppresses entry, so one capex story cannot describe both ends.
poles: high capex plus licensure blocks entry
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: apply the low-capex oversupply read to tattoo/nail and the high-capex-plus-licensure suppression read to med spa

conflict_axes.name: structural_cost_step_vs_weak_pricing_power
conflict_axes.description: The 2025 nail W-2 cost step lands on top of already-weak nail pricing power, and reading either alone understates the compounded squeeze.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: stack the structural W-2 cost increase on the weak pricing power to get the compounded 2025 nail margin compression

conflict_axes.name: estimate_labeling_vs_decisiveness
conflict_axes.description: Rigorous estimate-not-actual labeling protects honesty but can make the analysis read as too hedged to act on.
poles: label every figure as an estimate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: label every figure but pair it with a confidence and a confirmation path so the read stays actionable without overclaiming a named business's revenue

conflict_axes.name: snapshot_stability_vs_trend_drift
conflict_axes.description: The ~25 equilibrium reads as stable, but rebounding enrollment, the playing-out nail W-2 squeeze, and nationally compounding med spa are moving the underlying forces.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: hold the 2026-06-30 snapshot as a dated baseline but let the review loop, not assumption, decide when drift has moved the equilibrium

edge_cases.description: Term-time student/youth traffic is projected as year-round baseline demand
edge_cases.trigger: peak-semester nail, brow, or fade volume is annualized without the academic-calendar dip
edge_cases.mitigation: discount youth-driven demand for the summer/break academic-calendar dip

edge_cases.description: Modesto discretionary-leakage logic is applied to recurring-essential formats Modesto does not draw
edge_cases.trigger: the fine-tier leakage ceiling is used to cap barber or nail capacity
edge_cases.mitigation: apply leakage only to the discretionary tier (premium med spa, luxury spa, specialty tattoo); recurring-essential spend stays local

edge_cases.description: The gray-market solo/home/Instagram operator class is ignored, treating the 25-business catalog as the full competitive field
edge_cases.trigger: saturation or share is read off the catalog alone with no below-threshold operators
edge_cases.mitigation: flag the unsized gray-market class drawing on the same distributor channels as a real share-fragmenting competitor and the reason coverage is a floor

edge_cases.description: A secondary Spa/Day Spa tag inflates a business's apparent saturation count
edge_cases.trigger: Bliss, Salon Two Zero Nine, or Organic Nails is tallied under both its primary and spa-secondary category
edge_cases.mitigation: use primary category as the spine and note where spa secondaries justify a higher spa count without double-counting the business

edge_cases.description: A med-spa entrant clears the medical-director and capital wall mid-snapshot, shifting the saturation read
edge_cases.trigger: a new physician-supervised med spa opens after the 2026-06-30 snapshot
edge_cases.mitigation: treat the entry as a review-loop trigger and re-run the med-spa saturation and white-space reads

workflow.description: Record the resident base, median income, and CSU Stanislaus youth population with cited magnitudes
workflow.gate: the resident, income, and CSU figures each have a public-fact magnitude and a source confidence

workflow.action: Map heritage event and youth demand
workflow.description: Tie each heritage community and the youth segment to the event-beauty and sub-category demand they anchor
workflow.gate: each of the four communities and the youth segment is tied to anchored demand with cited shares

workflow.description: Classify the demand into recurring-essential and discretionary tiers with cadence and labeled tickets
workflow.gate: both tiers are named with cadence and ticket range and the leak/gate consequence is assigned to the discretionary tier

workflow.description: Derive the recurring-chair pool as population x frequency x labeled ticket, framed as a demand-volume estimate
workflow.gate: the pool is stated estimate-not-actual with its derivation, framing, confidence, and confirmation path

workflow.description: Derive each band as benchmark x size signal, paired with its cost/margin caveat
workflow.gate: every band is estimate-not-actual with a size signal, confidence, and cost/margin pairing

workflow.description: Set the cataloged count against population per 10k and national benchmarks with the floor caveat
workflow.gate: the per-10k figures, divisor, floor caveat, and nail-gap correction are all stated

workflow.action: Read the demand-governed equilibrium and per-sub-category ceilings
workflow.description: Set each sub-category's catalog count against its realistic ceiling and a crowded/balanced/white-space read
workflow.gate: each major sub-category has a count, ceiling, and saturation read consistent with the demand cap

workflow.action: Apply the capex spectrum and licensing barrier
workflow.description: Split low-capex from medical-capex sub-categories and identify the binding med-spa entry wall
workflow.gate: the low-capex band, the med-spa capex band, and the medical-director gate are stated and tied to the med-spa count

workflow.action: Rank white-space and apply the entry wall
workflow.description: Order the defensible openings and the do-not-add list, marking each white-space viable only after its entry wall clears
workflow.gate: the do-not-add list and three+ ranked openings are given, each white-space with a capital-and-licensure qualifier

workflow.description: Combine saturation, white-space, the nail W-2 squeeze, and the entry wall into an add/avoid call
workflow.gate: the verdict refuses any demand-true but cost-gated addition and names the do-not-add sub-categories

workflow.action: Set the market review cadence and triggers
workflow.description: Define the refresh cadence and material-change triggers routing back to pool sizing and saturation
workflow.gate: a cadence and a trigger list routing to SERVICE_DEMAND_POOL and saturation exist

priority_rationale: The demand base, heritage event demand, youth demand, and the recurring-vs-discretionary split are foundational because pool sizing, saturation, and white-space all read from them; the service-demand pool precedes the per-sub-category bands, the per-business-average correction, and the per-10k saturation it constrains; saturation, the capex/licensing entry wall, the labor model and the nail W-2 squeeze build on the demand and band layers; Modesto leakage, online/at-home substitution and the gray-market floor trim or qualify the equilibrium; the revenue-honesty and coverage-floor guardrails govern every dollar and density expression; and the go/no-go verdict plus the review loop come last because they compose all upstream reads into a decision and a self-correcting refresh.

dominance_rules.rule: The revenue-honesty guardrail dominates any pressure for a single decisive named-business number
dominance_rules.rationale: no per-business revenue is public, so an over-decisive figure for a named shop would be a fabrication
dominance_rules.trigger: a request for a named business's revenue or a single market number
dominance_rules.action: answer only with a labeled estimate (benchmark x size signal) plus confidence and confirmation path

dominance_rules.rule: The capital-and-licensure gate dominates a demand-true med-spa white-space opening
dominance_rules.rationale: the physician medical-director structure and six-figure capex can make a high-demand format un-enterable
dominance_rules.trigger: a med-spa or premium opening is judged attractive on demand alone
dominance_rules.action: mark it a no-go until the medical-director and capital entry wall clears

dominance_rules.rule: The per-sub-category typical band dominates the per-business average
dominance_rules.rationale: the per-business mean is tail-driven and not a typical business
dominance_rules.trigger: the per-business average is used to characterize a typical operator
dominance_rules.action: replace it with the typical-business placement within each sub-category band and label the mean low-confidence

dominance_rules.rule: The coverage floor dominates a thin per-10k ratio read as headroom
dominance_rules.rationale: excluded chains, counters, and gray-market operators make the independents-only ratio understate true density
dominance_rules.trigger: a thin per-10k ratio like nail 0.97-vs-3.4 is cited as room to grow
dominance_rules.action: flag it a counting-method artifact and read the sub-category as locally crowded

dominance_rules.rule: The Modesto ceiling dominates demand math for discretionary high-ticket formats
dominance_rules.rationale: cross-shopping leaks premium aesthetics, luxury spa, and specialty tattoo to the larger neighbor regardless of local demand
dominance_rules.trigger: a premium med-spa or luxury-spa addition is justified on Turlock demand alone
dominance_rules.action: cap the discretionary format at its leakage-lowered ceiling and weight the recapture difficulty

dominance_rules.rule: The compounded nail squeeze dominates a single-force nail margin read
dominance_rules.rationale: the 2025 W-2 cost step and weak pricing power must be stacked, not read in isolation
dominance_rules.trigger: nail margin is assessed on either the W-2 step or pricing power alone
dominance_rules.action: stack the structural cost increase on the weak pricing power for the compounded compression read

dominance_rules.rule: The recurring-essential floor dominates the count while the discretionary tier carries the leakage risk
dominance_rules.rationale: the count is demand-governed by the recurring pool; leakage and elasticity live in the discretionary tier
dominance_rules.trigger: the count is attributed to discretionary demand or leakage is applied to recurring formats
dominance_rules.action: anchor the count to the recurring floor and locate leakage/margin risk in the discretionary tier

dominance_rules.rule: Demand-governance dominates supply-chain explanations of the count
dominance_rules.rationale: the demand ceiling, not supply-chain friction, sets the number; capex explains mix and margin only
dominance_rules.trigger: the ~25 count is attributed to supply-chain ease or friction
dominance_rules.action: attribute the count to the demand ceiling and use capex/licensure to explain mix and margin

dominance_rules.rule: A flagged low-confidence input dominates a confident downstream conclusion built on it
dominance_rules.rationale: a conclusion cannot be more certain than its weakest load-bearing input
dominance_rules.trigger: the Modesto leakage magnitude or a benchmark band carries a conclusion above its own confidence
dominance_rules.action: cap the conclusion's confidence at that of its weakest input and name the confirmation source

anti_rework_rules.rule: Size the recurring service-demand pool before reading saturation or building per-sub-category bands
anti_rework_rules.prevents: deriving saturation and bands against a demand pool that later moves, forcing a full re-derivation

anti_rework_rules.rule: Label every dollar figure estimate-not-actual at the moment it is written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a later honesty sweep that must re-caveat figures already quoted as facts for a named business

anti_rework_rules.rule: Report every per-10k ratio as a floor, noting the excluded chains/counters/gray-market, before reading it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a thin ratio being misread as headroom and a saturation conclusion that must be redone

anti_rework_rules.rule: Apply the capital-and-licensure entry wall while ranking white-space, not after recommending it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: recommending a med-spa or premium opening that the medical-director or capital gate then voids

anti_rework_rules.rule: Read saturation off primary category, noting spa secondaries, before counting
anti_rework_rules.prevents: double-counted spa-secondary businesses inflating a saturation read that must be re-tallied

anti_rework_rules.rule: Stack the nail W-2 cost step on weak pricing power the first time nail margin is assessed
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a single-force nail margin read that must be reworked once the compounding is surfaced

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag the med-spa ~$1.4M and nail ~$34/capita national benchmarks as estimates the first time they appear
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a national-benchmark-as-fact drift that a later pass must re-label across the analysis

anti_rework_rules.rule: Assign Modesto leakage to the discretionary tier only when the demand split is first drawn
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a later correction once leakage is wrongly applied to recurring-essential formats

anti_rework_rules.rule: Name the confirmation path on every low-confidence figure (leakage, capture, bands) as it is stated
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a later pass to attach confirmation sources to numbers already published without them

iteration_protocol.trigger: a census/ACS demographic or CSU Stanislaus enrollment refresh lands
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the demand base and heritage/youth demand and re-size the service-demand pool

iteration_protocol.trigger: a med spa or nail/barber/tattoo business opens or closes in the catalog
iteration_protocol.action: re-tally the per-10k and per-sub-category saturation reads and the white-space ranking

iteration_protocol.trigger: the 2025 nail W-2 cost step settles into observable absorption
iteration_protocol.action: update the nail squeeze read and re-assess nail saturation and the go/no-go verdict

iteration_protocol.trigger: a national personal-care density or revenue benchmark updates
iteration_protocol.action: refresh the per-10k comparison and the per-sub-category revenue bands

iteration_protocol.trigger: a CA medical-director, corporate-practice, or worker-classification rule changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-price the entry wall and re-issue any affected go/no-go verdicts

iteration_protocol.trigger: a Turlock-vs-Modesto leakage study or a chair-rent/capex benchmark becomes available
iteration_protocol.action: replace the leakage and labor/capex estimates with measured figures and re-derive the affected reads

iteration_protocol.trigger: a gray-market sizing or licensing-roster cross-check becomes available
iteration_protocol.action: size the below-catalog operator class and refresh the coverage-floor read

iteration_protocol.trigger: an actual revenue datum (e.g., local sales-tax or distribution data) becomes available
iteration_protocol.action: replace the affected benchmark estimates with measured figures under the honesty guardrail and re-derive the per-business read
